verses.text: Now the whole world had one language and a common form of speech.
And as people journeyed eastward, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.
And they said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks and bake them thoroughly." So they used brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar.
"Come," they said, "let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth."
Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of men were building.
And the LORD said, "If they have begun to do this as one people speaking the same language, then nothing they devise will be beyond them.
Come, let Us go down and confuse their language, so that they will not understand one another's speech."
So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city.
That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world, and from that place the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.
This is the account of Shem. Two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, he became the father of Arphaxad.
And after he had become the father of Arphaxad, Shem lived 500 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Arphaxad was 35 years old, he became the father of Shelah.
And after he had become the father of Shelah, Arphaxad lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Shelah was 30 years old, he became the father of Eber.
And after he had become the father of Eber, Shelah lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Eber was 34 years old, he became the father of Peleg.
And after he had become the father of Peleg, Eber lived 430 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Peleg was 30 years old, he became the father of Reu.
And after he had become the father of Reu, Peleg lived 209 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Reu was 32 years old, he became the father of Serug.
And after he had become the father of Serug, Reu lived 207 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Serug was 30 years old, he became the father of Nahor.
And after he had become the father of Nahor, Serug lived 200 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Nahor was 29 years old, he became the father of Terah.
And after he had become the father of Terah, Nahor lived 119 years and had other sons and daughters.
When Terah was 70 years old, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
This is the account of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran became the father of Lot.
During his father Terah's lifetime, Haran died in his native land, in Ur of the Chaldeans.
And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. Abram's wife was named Sarai, and Nahor's wife was named Milcah; she was the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah.
But Sarai was barren; she had no children.

And Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai the wife of Abram, and they set out from Ur of the Chaldeans for the land of Canaan. But when they arrived in Haran, they settled there.
Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Narrative of beginnings (Genesis 1-11): creation, the first family, the flood and the nations, with genealogies
context.audience: Israel, God’s covenant people, learning who their God is, where the world came from and what went wrong with it
context.setting: “Now the whole world had one language and a common form of speech” (v.1). People settle on a plain in the land of Shinar and make baked bricks with tar for mortar (vv.2-3). “Come,” they say, “let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth” (v.4). “Then the LORD came down to see the city and the tower” (v.5). He confuses their language, scatters them, and they stop building; “that is why it is called Babel” (vv.7-9). The chapter then follows Shem’s line for ten generations to Terah, whose sons are Abram, Nahor and Haran (vv.10-27). Haran dies in Ur of the Chaldeans; “Sarai was barren; she had no children” (v.30). Terah takes Abram, Sarai and his grandson Lot and sets out from Ur for Canaan, but they settle in Haran, and Terah dies there (vv.31-32).
context.custom: Mesopotamia had no stone, so cities were built of mud brick, and the best bricks were baked in kilns and set in bitumen. Each great city had a ziggurat, a stepped temple tower; Babylon’s was called Etemenanki, ‘house of the foundation of heaven and earth.’ Its name in Akkadian, Bab-ili, means ‘gate of the god’; Genesis hears it as balal, ‘to confuse.’ There is irony in v.5: the tower meant to reach heaven is so small that God must come down to see it.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 12 tells how the LORD called Abram to leave his country for a land He would show him, with the promise that all families of the earth would be blessed through him.
context.timelineBible: At Pentecost the Spirit gave the apostles other tongues, and every nation heard “the wonders of God” (Acts 2:11) in its own language, a reversal of Babel. Stephen says God appeared to Abraham “while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran” (Acts 7:2). Revelation’s Babylon, the proud city that falls, carries the memory of this one (Revelation 18:2).

translation.meaning: Lip, and so speech or language. The whole world had ‘one lip.’
Name, fame, reputation. The builders want to make a name for themselves; in the next chapter God promises to make Abram’s name great (12:2). It is also the name of Noah’s son Shem.
To mix, confuse. A play on Babel, the city’s name.

gospelParallels.note: Each one heard them speaking in his own language.
God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.
Jesus’ line through Abraham, Terah, Eber and Shem.

otBackground.note: I will restore pure lips to the peoples.
I will ascend to the heavens; I will make myself like the Most High.
Terah lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods.

mapCoords.placeName: Babel in the land of Shinar (Babylon)

overview.summary: People build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves, but the LORD confuses their language and scatters them; then the line of Shem leads to Terah, who sets out from Ur with Abram, Sarai and Lot and settles in Haran.
overview.settingLine: The plain of Shinar, and the road from Ur to Haran.
overview.placeName: Babel in the land of Shinar (Babylon)

history.t: Stepped temple towers in every great city.
Both cities honored the moon god.

customs.t: Mud brick fired hard, with tar for mortar.
Lasting fame was the hope of kings.

archaeology.t: Babylon’s ziggurat, rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II; only its foundations remain.
Leonard Woolley excavated Ur (1922-34), with its ziggurat and royal tombs.

overview.discussion: The builders wanted to make a name for themselves (v.4); in the next chapter God promises to make Abram’s name great (12:2). Where am I trying to build my own name instead of receiving what God gives?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters (1-25 in the app so far). Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham and his family.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

historicalImage.caption: The Tower of Babel, by Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563, Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna). Bruegel built his tower like the Colosseum in Rome, unfinished and already leaning: “let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens” (Genesis 11:4).
historicalImage.credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

currentImage.caption: The ziggurat of Ur in southern Iraq, built about 2100 BC for the moon god Nanna and partly restored in the 1980s. Stepped temple towers of mud brick like this are the likely background of the tower of Babel, built with “brick instead of stone, and tar instead of mortar” (Genesis 11:3).
